keep: The idea is named in the first three sentences: two plates in acid, both plates turn to lead sulphate and the acid is used up on discharge, and charging runs it backwards.

Each misconception the brief names for lesson 1 has a puzzle with its own wrong pick: electrons through the acid and ions as electron carriers (screen 6), the acid as a bath (screen 4), a bigger cell giving more volts (screen 12).
One worked number from a stated rule: the 2.04 V gap from +1.685 V and −0.356 V, with the sign slip (1.33 V) as screen 10's wrong pick; and 12 cells × 2.1 V = 25.2 V for a 24 V battery.

The picture follows the brief: cut-away cell, white lead sulphate on both plates, acid dots leaving the liquid, electrons round the wire and only ions in the acid, the ladder, the size slider that leaves the voltmeter still, and the 1/6/12/24 series stepper. No chemical formulae anywhere.

The analogy (pumped storage) reproduces both halves of the result, used up and put back, and volts from what, ampere-hours from how much; its break is the honest one (nothing moves plate to plate, both plates change where they stand).
fix: Causal step skipped: why the ions move at all. Add one sentence: as one plate frees electrons and the other takes them in, the liquid next to each would build up charge, and the ions drifting through the acid keep it balanced, which is what lets the current flow round the loop.
Causal step skipped: why a charger must sit above the cell's voltage. Say it must push current in against the cell's own push, so it needs more than the cell's voltage.

The mechanism interactive has no setting where the cause is absent. Give the builder one: with the load switch open and no charger, no current flows and the plates and acid hold still (a real cell left open discharges itself, far too slowly to see, said in ignores).
Talks about where things come from: 'Textbooks add that …' and 'Textbooks list them …' break Dan's 20 Oct plain-writing rule. Say the facts plainly.

False absolute: 'Plate size never enters that sum'. True, but say it plainly: 'Plate size is not in that sum.' 'A battery has no off switch' is wrong for a bank with an isolator: say the cells themselves cannot be switched off.

Paragraph 4 carries six things (2 V, rested 2.1 V, size, series, the simplification, the puzzle). Move charging and the 2 V into paragraph 3, so paragraph 4 is size, series, the model's limits and the puzzle.
The course-puzzle sentence is vague. Say what this idea gives it: a healthy voltage says what the plates are made of, not how much of them can still react.
Footnotes: five, one on a sentence the next sentence's footnote already covers. Drop [^2] (the positive plate) so the lesson carries four.
Several sentences run past 20 words with chained clauses (the opening 'As it discharges, …' at 22). Split them, one idea per sentence.

The builder needs ion directions and the reverse on charge: on discharge the acid's positive ions drift towards the lead dioxide plate and its negative ions towards the lead plate, the other way on charge. And each SHOW screen's words must end on what its finished picture shows, under about 90 words, so the read-through makes sense with no controls.
Screen 8's third choice ('tops up the plates' electrons') is not a slip anyone makes. Use the plausible one: the acid strengthens but the plates stay lead sulphate.

shape.workedExampleWithRealNumbers: yes (2.04 V gap; 24 V battery = 12 cells, 25.2 V rested)
shape.misconceptionShownFailing: yes: electrons through acid, acid as a bath, bigger is more volts, each on the picture and a puzzle
